slides.direction: The root-cause box of section 22.9, shown when the demonstration reaches `--everything`.
slides.text:
Observed behavior : After migrate import --everything, main is "ahead 5, behind 1" of origin/main and
                    the log shows the first commit twice, as e6c7da2 and as c66100a.
Git state         : origin/main still names c66100a. Local main descends from e6c7da2, a rewritten
                    copy of it. The two histories share no commit.
Mechanism         : --everything put the pushed root commit in scope. The .gitattributes line was
                    added in the first commit in scope, which changed its tree and therefore its ID,
                    and the ID of every descendant.
Root cause        : A history rewrite that included published commits.
Why Git does this : A commit ID is a hash of the commit's content, parents included (Chapter 6).
                    A different first commit cannot have the same descendants.
Correct fix       : Not pushed yet: return both branches to their previous positions from their
                    reflogs and migrate with the branch named instead (Lab 15.4).
Prevention        : Run migrate info with the same scope options first and read the commit count.
                    Use --everything only for a planned rewrite of published history.

slides.direction: 🟡 CAUTION: `git lfs migrate import`, default scope. It rewrites unpushed commits; the working tree is left with pointers. Preview: `migrate info` with the same options. Recovery: the branch reflog.

rows: Included per month: 10 GiB of storage and 10 GiB of bandwidth on Free and Pro; 250 GiB of each on Team and Enterprise Cloud
Beyond that, usage is metered and billed
"Previously, Git LFS billing used pre-paid data packs. These have been removed and replaced with metered billing."
Advice to "buy a data pack" is out of date
Every pushed version is stored in full: "If you make a 1 byte change and push the file again, you'll use another 500 MB of storage"
Storage grows with the number of versions, not with the size of the latest one
Downloads use bandwidth; uploads do not. Downloads by GitHub Actions count
A CI matrix that pulls the same model in every job multiplies bandwidth
"Bandwidth and storage usage always count against the repository owner's account"; pushes to forks count "against the parent repository's bandwidth and storage quotas"
The owner pays for what contributors and forks do
When the quota is used up and no payment method is on file, clones "will only retrieve the pointer files" and you "will not be able to push new files back up"
An exhausted quota looks exactly like a machine without the client

After removing files from LFS, "the Git LFS objects still exist on the remote storage and will continue to count toward your Git LFS storage quota"; to remove them, "delete and recreate the repository", or contact Support
Storage does not shrink when history does

slides.direction: "Unverified." Per-GiB prices for metered LFS usage are not stated on the billing page that was read, and the research report behind the course records a conflict between GitHub's pricing page and its billing documentation about data packs. The textbook gives no prices, and neither does this video.

Training data and model weights that change with every run
Each version is stored whole and billed; nothing is ever freed
DVC, which keeps small metafiles in Git and the data in a remote you control; or a model registry, with the Git commit recorded beside each model version
Data that must be deletable (personal data, licensed data)
Removing a file from LFS on GitHub does not delete the object
Storage with retention and deletion controls
Models and datasets published for others
Consumers need the client, and your bandwidth pays for their downloads
The Hugging Face Hub, pinning the revision you download; or GitHub Releases for binaries that accompany a tag
Contributors or CI that cannot be relied on to have the client
Pointer files in place of content, silently
Any of the above; or a download step with a checksum

items: git lfs track and a new commit to fix a rejected push. Root cause: the large blob is still in an earlier commit of the push; only migrate import on those commits replaces it.

migrate import --everything to "catch the other branch". Root cause: it puts published commits in scope, and the first rewritten commit changes the ID of every descendant, so local history no longer shares a commit with the remote.

params.title: migrate import with the default scope

slides.lead: You should now be able to say:
items: git lfs migrate import rewrites the commits in scope into pointer commits with new IDs; by default the scope is the unpushed commits of the current branch.
After an import the working tree holds a pointer until git lfs checkout, and .git shrinks only after the reflog expires and a collection runs.
A raw blob on an LFS path is found by git lfs fsck --pointers and fixed forward with git add --renormalize; a pointer without its object is fixed by git lfs push --all from whoever has it.

GitHub blocks large files by commit, stores every pushed LFS version in full, bills the repository owner, and does not free LFS storage when history is rewritten; I state the numbers from the documentation and no prices.
LFS suits a few mid-sized binaries that change rarely; for per-run weights, deletable data and published models the textbook names other stores.

slides.body: Read sections 22.9 to 22.14 of Chapter 22 and do the Practice section, 22.16.
That's the end of submodules, subtrees and Git LFS, and you can now plan a migration, read three LFS errors from their messages, and say when LFS is the wrong tool.

beats.text: You can answer the first question now. Git LFS keeps large files outside Git and leaves a small pointer file in their place, but only for files added after tracking began. Here the blob is in a commit being pushed, and deleting the file added a commit without removing one. The engineer's next attempt is git lfs track, and a new commit. Still rejected, for the same reason.
beats.tele: You can answer the first question now. Git LFS keeps large files outside Git and leaves a small pointer file in their place, but only for files added after tracking began. Here the blob is in a commit being pushed, and deleting the file added a commit without removing one. The engineer's next attempt is `git lfs track`, and a new commit. Still rejected, for the same reason.

beats.text: The tool that does help is a history rewrite: new commits that take the place of the old ones. And the same tool, with one extra flag that promises to "catch everything", leaves a branch that's five commits ahead of the server and one behind it, sharing not a single commit with what the team has.
beats.tele: The tool that does help is a history rewrite: new commits that take the place of the old ones. And the same tool, with one extra flag that promises to "catch everything", leaves a branch that's five commits ahead of the server and one behind it, sharing not a single commit with what the team has.

beats.text: The second question has an answer that surprises people who think in Git terms: on the hosting side, storage doesn't shrink when history does. Hold on to that second question. Its answer is one row of a table.
beats.tele: The second question has an answer that surprises people who think in Git terms: on the hosting side, storage doesn't shrink when history does. Hold on to that second question. Its answer is one row of a table.

beats.text: Welcome back to Git and GitHub Deep Mastery. Pull up a chair. This is the last video on LFS, and it has four parts. git lfs migrate, for files that are already in history. Three errors that you'll meet, each recognised from its message. GitHub's file limits and how it bills for LFS, stated from its documentation. And the judgement call: when LFS is the wrong tool and what the textbook names instead.
beats.tele: Welcome back to Git and GitHub Deep Mastery. Pull up a chair. This is the last video on LFS, and it has four parts. `git lfs migrate`, for files that are already in history. Three errors that you'll meet, each recognised from its message. GitHub's file limits and how it bills for LFS, stated from its documentation. And the judgement call: when LFS is the wrong tool and what the textbook names instead.

beats.text: Everything about rewriting history from the rebase module applies here: new commit IDs, and the difference between published and unpublished commits. Two of the replays are volatile and will be marked on screen.
beats.tele: Everything about rewriting history from the rebase module applies here: new commit IDs, and the difference between published and unpublished commits. Two of the replays are volatile and will be marked on screen.

beats.text: say what git lfs migrate import does to commit IDs, the working tree and the size of .git;
beats.tele: say what `git lfs migrate import` does to commit IDs, the working tree and the size of `.git`;

beats.text: plan a migration of a shared repository as a history rewrite;
beats.tele: plan a migration of a shared repository as a history rewrite;

beats.text: diagnose three LFS errors from their messages: a missing object, a file that should have been a pointer, a file tracked too late;
beats.tele: diagnose three LFS errors from their messages: a missing object, a file that should have been a pointer, a file tracked too late;

beats.text: state GitHub's file limits and the LFS billing model as the cited section gives them;
beats.tele: state GitHub's file limits and the LFS billing model as the cited section gives them;

beats.text: decide when LFS is the wrong tool and name the alternative the section gives.
beats.tele: decide when LFS is the wrong tool and name the alternative the section gives.

beats.text: git lfs migrate has three modes.
beats.tele: `git lfs migrate` has three modes.

beats.text: info reads history and reports sizes by file extension. It changes nothing. 🟢 SAFE.
beats.tele: `info` reads history and reports sizes by file extension. It changes nothing. 🟢 SAFE.

beats.text: import is a history rewrite. 🟡 CAUTION for the default scope: it replaces matching blobs by pointers in every commit in scope, adds the .gitattributes line, and gives every rewritten commit and all of its descendants a new ID.
beats.tele: `import` is a history rewrite. 🟡 CAUTION for the default scope: it replaces matching blobs by pointers in every commit in scope, adds the `.gitattributes` line, and gives every rewritten commit and all of its descendants a new ID.

beats.text: export is the reverse rewrite: pointers become ordinary blobs again in the commits in scope.
beats.tele: `export` is the reverse rewrite: pointers become ordinary blobs again in the commits in scope.

beats.text: Scope is the dangerous option. By default all three modes look only at the current branch, and only at commits that are on no remote. That default is the safe one: nothing that anyone else has is rewritten. Name further branches as arguments to include their unpushed commits.
beats.tele: Scope is the dangerous option. By default all three modes look only at the current branch, and only at commits that are on no remote. That default is the safe one: nothing that anyone else has is rewritten. Name further branches as arguments to include their unpushed commits.

beats.text: --everything means every commit reachable from every local and remote ref, including commits that are already on the remote.
beats.tele: `--everything` means every commit reachable from every local and remote ref, including commits that are already on the remote.

beats.text: 🔴 DANGEROUS when followed by a forced push: it rewrites published history.
beats.tele: 🔴 DANGEROUS when followed by a forced push: it rewrites published history.

beats.text: Back to the default scope. Two things about the state import leaves surprise people. First, the working tree file is a pointer afterwards, even with the filter installed. The command's own help says this is normal and names the remedy, git lfs checkout. Second, the repository didn't get smaller.
beats.tele: Back to the default scope. Two things about the state `import` leaves surprise people. First, the working tree file is a pointer afterwards, even with the filter installed. The command's own help says this is normal and names the remedy, `git lfs checkout`. Second, the repository didn't get smaller.

beats.text: The old commits are off the branch and still in the reflog, Git's local journal of where a branch has been. So the old blobs are still in the object database until the reflog entries expire and a garbage collection runs. And the bytes haven't left your disk either: they are in .git/lfs/objects now, once per version.
beats.tele: The old commits are off the branch and still in the reflog, Git's local journal of where a branch has been. So the old blobs are still in the object database until the reflog entries expire and a garbage collection runs. And the bytes haven't left your disk either: they are in `.git/lfs/objects` now, once per version.

beats.text: When the large files are already on the remote, a rewrite of published history is what you need, and it's an operation with a plan, not a command. Everyone stops pushing. One person rewrites and pushes with --force-with-lease, the forced push that first checks what the server has. Everyone else re-clones or resets. Old clones that push again bring the blobs back.
beats.tele: When the large files are already on the remote, a rewrite of published history is what you need, and it's an operation with a plan, not a command. Everyone stops pushing. One person rewrites and pushes with `--force-with-lease`, the forced push that first checks what the server has. Everyone else re-clones or resets. Old clones that push again bring the blobs back.

beats.text: There's also git lfs migrate import --no-rewrite, which converts files in one new commit without touching earlier ones. It has the limit you would expect: the old blobs stay in history, so it doesn't help with a push that's rejected for a large file.
beats.tele: There's also `git lfs migrate import --no-rewrite`, which converts files in one new commit without touching earlier ones. It has the limit you would expect: the old blobs stay in history, so it doesn't help with a push that's rejected for a large file.

beats.text: Three errors, one family. In each, a path that .gitattributes assigns to LFS, the blob in Git, and the object in the LFS store don't agree.
beats.tele: Three errors, one family. In each, a path that `.gitattributes` assigns to LFS, the blob in Git, and the object in the LFS store don't agree.

beats.text: The file was committed before the pattern was tracked: the blob is the raw file.
beats.tele: The file was committed before the pattern was tracked: the blob is the raw file.

beats.text: A commit was made on a machine without the filter: the blob is the raw file again, reached from the other side.
beats.tele: A commit was made on a machine without the filter: the blob is the raw file again, reached from the other side.

beats.text: The pointer was pushed and the object wasn't: the blob is a correct pointer to content that the remote doesn't have. The textbook points out the family resemblance to the unpushed submodule commit: a reference was published without the thing it refers to.
beats.tele: The pointer was pushed and the object wasn't: the blob is a correct pointer to content that the remote doesn't have. The textbook points out the family resemblance to the unpushed submodule commit: a reference was published without the thing it refers to.

beats.text: GitHub. Limits and billing are platform behavior. Hold that for the on-screen segment, where every number is read from the textbook's quotation of the documentation.
beats.tele: GitHub. Limits and billing are platform behavior. Hold that for the on-screen segment, where every number is read from the textbook's quotation of the documentation.

beats.text: When not to use LFS. LFS fits a modest number of mid-sized binary files that change rarely and must be versioned together with the code: reference checkpoints for tests, small fixtures, images and design assets. The table of section 22.13 lists five situations in which it's the wrong tool. You'll read it at the end of the demonstration.
beats.tele: When not to use LFS. LFS fits a modest number of mid-sized binary files that change rarely and must be versioned together with the code: reference checkpoints for tests, small fixtures, images and design assets. The table of section 22.13 lists five situations in which it's the wrong tool. You'll read it at the end of the demonstration.

beats.text: Use the coat check for the three errors.
beats.tele: Use the coat check for the three errors.

beats.text: Tracked too late, or committed without the filter: somebody walked past the ticket desk and hung the coat itself on the ticket rail. The rail was built for tickets. Everyone who comes later finds a coat where a ticket should be.
beats.tele: Tracked too late, or committed without the filter: somebody walked past the ticket desk and hung the coat itself on the ticket rail. The rail was built for tickets. Everyone who comes later finds a coat where a ticket should be.

beats.text: Pointer pushed, object not: a ticket was sent to the other building, and the coat it names never left yours. Whoever presents the ticket there's told that no such coat exists.
beats.tele: Pointer pushed, object not: a ticket was sent to the other building, and the coat it names never left yours. Whoever presents the ticket there's told that no such coat exists.

beats.text: For migrate import, picture reprinting the history books so that every page that used to have a coat stapled to it now has a ticket, with the coats moved to the cloakroom. Reprinted pages have new page numbers, and so does every page after them. The old print run is still in your storeroom until you clear it out. The analogy breaks on purpose at the hosting side: clearing your storeroom doesn't empty the host's cloakroom.
beats.tele: For `migrate import`, picture reprinting the history books so that every page that used to have a coat stapled to it now has a ticket, with the coats moved to the cloakroom. Reprinted pages have new page numbers, and so does every page after them. The old print run is still in your storeroom until you clear it out. The analogy breaks on purpose at the hosting side: clearing your storeroom doesn't empty the host's cloakroom.

beats.text: Try it now, on paper, thirty seconds. Draw five commits in a row. The first is already on the remote. The second and third each add a model, the fourth doesn't touch it, and the fifth adds another. Circle every commit whose ID you predict will change.
beats.tele: Try it now, on paper, thirty seconds. Draw five commits in a row. The first is already on the remote. The second and third each add a model, the fourth doesn't touch it, and the fifth adds another. Circle every commit whose ID you predict will change.

beats.text: Check your circles. The commit that was already on the remote kept its ID. The four above it are new commits with the old messages, authors and dates. Look at the fourth row: that commit didn't touch the model, and its ID changed anyway, because a commit ID is a hash that includes the parent. If you left that one out, you're in good company.
beats.tele: Check your circles. The commit that was already on the remote kept its ID. The four above it are new commits with the old messages, authors and dates. Look at the fourth row: that commit didn't touch the model, and its ID changed anyway, because a commit ID is a hash that includes the parent. If you left that one out, you're in good company.

beats.text: Note the scope it chose by itself. The line "Examining commits" ends at four of four. main is four commits ahead of origin/main, so four commits were examined. 3.8 megabytes of .onnx in three files.
beats.tele: Note the scope it chose by itself. The line "Examining commits" ends at four of four. `main` is four commits ahead of `origin/main`, so four commits were examined. 3.8 megabytes of `.onnx` in three files.

beats.text: You predicted this one on paper: how many of the five commit IDs change?
beats.tele: You predicted this one on paper: how many of the five commit IDs change?

beats.text: Four. c66100a, which was already on the remote, kept its ID.
beats.tele: Four. `c66100a`, which was already on the remote, kept its ID.

beats.text: The rewritten first model commit, b1b921b, adds .gitattributes and a three-line file where the model was. The rest of the snippet shows three pointer blobs of 132 bytes where the branch reached three large blobs.
beats.tele: The rewritten first model commit, `b1b921b`, adds `.gitattributes` and a three-line file where the model was. The rest of the snippet shows three pointer blobs of 132 bytes where the branch reached three large blobs.

beats.text: Now the first surprise. A quick quiz: after the import, is the model file in the working tree its full size, or 132 bytes? Say it out loud.
beats.tele: Now the first surprise. A quick quiz: after the import, is the model file in the working tree its full size, or 132 bytes? Say it out loud.

beats.text: 132 bytes, a minus in the listing. After git lfs checkout, the real 1,300,000 bytes. The second surprise: the repository didn't get smaller.
beats.tele: 132 bytes, a minus in the listing. After `git lfs checkout`, the real 1,300,000 bytes. The second surprise: the repository didn't get smaller.

beats.text: Before the expiry, the reflog still names 8b13104, the old tip, and three blobs of seven-digit size are still in the object database. After it, they are gone from Git's store.
beats.tele: Before the expiry, the reflog still names `8b13104`, the old tip, and three blobs of seven-digit size are still in the object database. After it, they are gone from Git's store.

beats.text: A flag that promises to catch everything looks like the answer.
beats.tele: A flag that promises to catch everything looks like the answer.

beats.text: Read the graph from the bottom: the root commit is now e6c7da2, a rewritten copy of the pushed root.
beats.tele: Read the graph from the bottom: the root commit is now `e6c7da2`, a rewritten copy of the pushed root.

beats.text: The local branches no longer share a commit with origin/main. That's the root-cause box on screen. Not pushed yet, so the fix is in the branch reflogs, and the lab walks through it.
beats.tele: The local branches no longer share a commit with `origin/main`. That's the root-cause box on screen. Not pushed yet, so the fix is in the branch reflogs, and the lab walks through it.

beats.text: New commit IDs again, above the same unchanged c66100a. Export doesn't delete the tracking line. It appends a line that switches the attributes off for the pattern.
beats.tele: New commit IDs again, above the same unchanged `c66100a`. Export doesn't delete the tracking line. It appends a line that switches the attributes off for the pattern.

beats.text: Predict what git status says about a file nobody edited. Say it out loud. I'll wait.
beats.tele: Predict what `git status` says about a file nobody edited. Say it out loud. I'll wait.

beats.text: Three symptoms of one cause. git lfs ls-files doesn't list the recording. The blob in HEAD is 48,000 bytes, the raw file. And git status reports the file as modified: the attributes now say "clean this path", the clean filter turns the working tree file into a pointer, and the pointer differs from the raw blob in the index. git lfs fsck --pointers names the problem: "should have been a pointer but was not".
beats.tele: Three symptoms of one cause. `git lfs ls-files` doesn't list the recording. The blob in HEAD is 48,000 bytes, the raw file. And `git status` reports the file as modified: the attributes now say "clean this path", the clean filter turns the working tree file into a pointer, and the pointer differs from the raw blob in the index. `git lfs fsck --pointers` names the problem: "should have been a pointer but was not".

beats.text: The forward fix. 🟡 CAUTION: git add --renormalize runs the path through the filter again and stages the result.
beats.tele: The forward fix. 🟡 CAUTION: `git add --renormalize` runs the path through the filter again and stages the result.

beats.text: The raw blob is still in the earlier commit. For a 48 kilobyte file that's acceptable. For a file that a host would reject, use git lfs migrate import on the unpushed commits instead.
beats.tele: The raw blob is still in the earlier commit. For a 48 kilobyte file that's acceptable. For a file that a host would reject, use `git lfs migrate import` on the unpushed commits instead.

beats.text: No filter, and the attribute line is there. The full 1,250,000 bytes went into Git as a blob. Asha, who has the filter, pulls.
beats.tele: No filter, and the attribute line is there. The full 1,250,000 bytes went into Git as a blob. Asha, who has the filter, pulls.

beats.text: "Bin 132 -> 1250000 bytes" in the pull's summary is the first sign.
beats.tele: "Bin 132 -> 1250000 bytes" in the pull's summary is the first sign.

beats.text: The same diagnosis as before, and the file is modified the moment it's checked out. The same fix, and the same limit: the large blob stays in the history that was pushed.
beats.tele: The same diagnosis as before, and the file is modified the moment it's checked out. The same fix, and the same limit: the large blob stays in the history that was pushed.

beats.text: Prevention is a server-side or CI check, because the failing machine is by definition one where the local setup is missing: a job that runs git lfs fsck --pointers and fails on a non-zero exit status.
beats.tele: Prevention is a server-side or CI check, because the failing machine is by definition one where the local setup is missing: a job that runs `git lfs fsck --pointers` and fails on a non-zero exit status.

beats.text: Here the hook was skipped with --no-verify. The pointer is in the remote's Git history. The object exists only in the author's local store. A teammate with a correctly installed client pulls.
beats.tele: Here the hook was skipped with `--no-verify`. The pointer is in the remote's Git history. The object exists only in the author's local store. A teammate with a correctly installed client pulls.

beats.text: "remote missing object", exit status 2, and a minus in the listing. The same failure through the smudge filter:
beats.tele: "remote missing object", exit status 2, and a minus in the listing. The same failure through the smudge filter:

beats.text: "Smudge error". Because the filter is required, a failing smudge fails the checkout: the file is absent, not silently wrong.
beats.tele: "Smudge error". Because the filter is `required`, a failing smudge fails the checkout: the file is absent, not silently wrong.

beats.text: The pointer names f8719e1. The remote's store has one file, and it isn't that one.
beats.tele: The pointer names `f8719e1`. The remote's store has one file, and it isn't that one.

beats.text: Whoever still has the object uploads it. Predict whether a plain git lfs push origin main does it. I'll wait.
beats.tele: Whoever still has the object uploads it. Predict whether a plain `git lfs push origin main` does it. I'll wait.

beats.text: No, and almost everyone expects a yes. The client skips objects of commits that the remote-tracking branch already contains.
beats.tele: No, and almost everyone expects a yes. The client skips objects of commits that the remote-tracking branch already contains.

beats.text: git lfs push --all origin main sends every object the branch references. If nobody has the object any more, the pointer is permanently dangling, and the only repair is a new commit with a file that exists.
beats.tele: `git lfs push --all origin main` sends every object the branch references. If nobody has the object any more, the pointer is permanently dangling, and the only repair is a new commit with a file that exists.

beats.text: Without LFS, the section quotes four limits.
beats.tele: Without LFS, the section quotes four limits.

beats.text: A warning from Git for a file larger than 50 mebibytes. "GitHub blocks files larger than 100 MiB". A file added through the browser "can be no larger than 25 MiB". And repositories should "remain small, ideally less than 1 GB, and less than 5 GB is strongly recommended". It adds a cap of 2 gigabytes for a single push. The block applies to any commit in the push that contains such a blob.
beats.tele: A warning from Git for a file larger than 50 mebibytes. "GitHub blocks files larger than 100 MiB". A file added through the browser "can be no larger than 25 MiB". And repositories should "remain small, ideally less than 1 GB, and less than 5 GB is strongly recommended". It adds a cap of 2 gigabytes for a single push. The block applies to any commit in the push that contains such a blob.

beats.text: With LFS, the maximum size of one LFS file depends on the plan: 2 gigabytes on GitHub Free and Pro, 4 gigabytes on Team, 5 gigabytes on Enterprise Cloud.
beats.tele: With LFS, the maximum size of one LFS file depends on the plan: 2 gigabytes on GitHub Free and Pro, 4 gigabytes on Team, 5 gigabytes on Enterprise Cloud.

beats.text: The last row is the answer to the storage-bill question, the one you were holding on to.
beats.tele: The last row is the answer to the storage-bill question, the one you were holding on to.

beats.text: The textbook notes that the versions, licences and stewardship of these tools changed during 2025 and 2026, and that the AI and ML workflows chapter gives the current facts with their sources.
beats.tele: The textbook notes that the versions, licences and stewardship of these tools changed during 2025 and 2026, and that the AI and ML workflows chapter gives the current facts with their sources.

beats.text: Five mistakes to watch for.
beats.tele: Five mistakes to watch for.

beats.text: git lfs track and a new commit to fix a rejected push. Root cause: the large blob is still in an earlier commit of the push; only migrate import on those commits replaces it.
beats.tele: `git lfs track` and a new commit to fix a rejected push. Root cause: the large blob is still in an earlier commit of the push; only `migrate import` on those commits replaces it.

beats.text: migrate import --everything to "catch the other branch". Root cause: it puts published commits in scope, and the first rewritten commit changes the ID of every descendant, so local history no longer shares a commit with the remote.
beats.tele: `migrate import --everything` to "catch the other branch". Root cause: it puts published commits in scope, and the first rewritten commit changes the ID of every descendant, so local history no longer shares a commit with the remote.

beats.text: Expecting .git to shrink right after a migration. Root cause: the old commits are still in the reflog and their blobs in the object database until expiry and a collection.

beats.text: git lfs push origin main to repair a missing object. Root cause: the client skips objects of commits that the remote-tracking branch already has; --all sends everything the branch references.
